opus-5.5.text:
I think the "mechanical person" framing smuggles in a lot of assumptions that don't really hold up when you look at how technology actually gets adopted. When people imagine robots, they picture something like a humanoid butler that walks into your kitchen and does everything a person would do, the way a person would do it. But if you look at the history of machines that do physical work, that's almost never how it goes.

Take a bulldozer. A bulldozer doesn't replace a guy with a shovel by being a really strong guy with a really big shovel. It's a totally different thing. It changes what earthmoving *is*. You reorganize the job site around it, you change how many people you need and what they do, and suddenly projects that would have been unthinkable become routine. Cars are similar. A car isn't a mechanical horse. It reshaped cities, supply chains, where people live. The value came from the system changing around the machine, not from the machine slotting neatly into the role of the thing it replaced.

I think robots will be like that. The interesting question isn't "when will we have a robot that can do everything a human can do in a human environment," it's "what happens when physical labor gets dramatically cheaper and more flexible, and how does the world reorganize around that?" That might mean robots that look nothing like people, working in settings designed for them, doing tasks in ways a human never would.

There's also a practical side, which is about deployment. If you think of the robot as a mechanical person, you're kind of stuck waiting for this all-or-nothing moment where it's good enough to replace a human outright. But cars and bulldozers both have a human in the loop. They're tools that amplify what a person can do. And I think that's a much more realistic path for robotics: you get systems that are useful with some human oversight, they get deployed, they collect data, they get better, and the scope of what they do autonomously keeps expanding. That flywheel is really what matters, and you get it much sooner if you stop insisting the robot has to be a drop-in human replacement from day one.

And frankly, I think the humanoid framing can make people both too pessimistic and too optimistic at the same time. Too pessimistic, because matching a human at everything is an incredibly high bar. Too optimistic, because it suggests the impact will be like adding more workers, when really the bigger effects are going to come from the second-order changes, the same way the biggest effects of the car weren't about horses at all.

r001.rationale: The response favors diverse, nonhuman robot forms and says they could work in settings designed for them, but it does not state that intelligence supporting those forms could achieve more than restricting robots to humanlike forms.

r002.rationale: It discusses deployment, human oversight, and physical work broadly, but does not explain that robots could enable remote data centers by eliminating the need for nearby human amenities.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the analogy I like to make is that when people imagine robots, they often imagine a kind of mechanical person, right? Something that looks like us, acts like us, has the same kind of general-purpose capability that we have. And I think that framing is actually a little misleading in terms of what the technology will actually look like and what it's going to be good for.

If you think about cars, a car is in some sense a mechanical horse. But nobody who builds cars is trying to make a horse. The car does something that a horse used to do, which is get you from point A to point B, but it does it in a way that's completely different and in many respects far better, because it's engineered around what the technology is actually good at. Same thing with a bulldozer. A bulldozer is doing something that people used to do with shovels, but it isn't a mechanical man holding a shovel. It's a completely different form factor that exploits what machines can do that people can't.

And I think that's how it's going to be for robots with AI. The things that make these systems powerful are not that they replicate human intelligence one-for-one. It's that they have properties humans don't have. They can share experience. If one robot learns something, every robot can learn it. They can run at different scales, they can have different embodiments, they can be in a lot of places at once. So the question that actually matters isn't "when do we get a mechanical person," it's "what does a machine that learns from experience and physically acts in the world make possible that wasn't possible before?" And the answer to that probably looks as different from a mechanical person as a car looks from a horse.

The other reason I like that framing is it keeps us honest about the goal. We're not trying to pass some test of humanlikeness. We're trying to build something useful. And a lot of the things that make robots hard right now — the long tail of situations, the physical variability of the world — those are challenges that get solved by learning from data at scale, not by making the robot look or think more like a person.

r001.rationale: The response says robots can have different embodiments and scales, and that machine capabilities can make possible things beyond a mechanical person, supporting the benefit of diverse physical forms.

r002.rationale: It mentions robots being in many places at once, but does not say they could enable data centers in remote locations or explain that they do not need nearby human amenities.

astra-6.text:
I think the analogy to a mechanical person brings along a lot of assumptions that aren't necessarily useful. You imagine something that has a person's motivations, a person's understanding of the world, and a person's ability to do essentially any task. But those things don't have to come as a package.

A bulldozer lets one person do an amount of physical work that would otherwise require many people. A car lets you move much faster than you could on foot. Neither does that by reproducing a human. They're machines that extend what we can do, and I think that's a useful way to think about robots as well.

Even if a robot has a humanoid form, that might simply be because our environments are built for human bodies. It can use the stairs, reach the shelves, and fit through the doors. That doesn't mean the right goal is to build a synthetic person. The goal could be to build a very useful machine that can learn how to perform a wide range of physical tasks. And then the questions become: What does it enable people to do? How reliable is it? How much does it cost? Those are much more productive questions than how closely it resembles us.

r001.rationale: The response says useful robots need not reproduce humans and could perform a wide range of physical tasks, but it does not state that intelligence supporting diverse physical forms could achieve more than limiting robots to humanlike forms.

r002.rationale: It does not mention remote data centers or robots’ lack of need for nearby human amenities.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the image of a robot as a mechanical person comes with a lot of assumptions that aren’t necessarily useful. You imagine something that has its own goals, that wants to do things, and that participates in society the way a person does. But that’s not really why we build machines. We build them to help us do things.

A bulldozer is enormously powerful. It can do physical work that no human could do, but we understand its purpose in terms of extending a person’s capabilities. A car lets you travel farther and faster. I think robots are much more naturally understood in that same way: as tools that let us accomplish things in the physical world.

That doesn’t mean they can’t be autonomous. You might tell a robot to clean up your kitchen, and it would need to figure out a lot of details for itself. But that autonomy is in service of something you want done. It doesn’t require us to think of the robot as a separate person. And I think that framing helps us ask a more useful question, which is: What capabilities would actually make this machine helpful?

r001.rationale: The response argues that robots are useful tools and need not be personlike, but does not state that intelligence spanning diverse physical forms could achieve more than limiting robots to humanlike forms.

r002.rationale: It gives examples of bulldozers, cars, and kitchen-cleaning robots, but does not mention remote data centers or the lack of need for nearby human amenities.
